Dictionaries and tools, used properly.front: The step of this stage that matters most for vocabulary
Dictionaries and tools, used properly.back: Moving to a Greek-to-Greek dictionary: an English gloss is an approximation, a Greek definition is the word’s own shape, and reading it is more input

Dictionaries and tools, used properly.front: Which tool answers “what form is this?”
Dictionaries and tools, used properly.back: Lexiscope — paste the inflected word, get the lemma and the full table

Dictionaries and tools, used properly.front: Which tool answers “how is this actually used?”
Dictionaries and tools, used properly.back: Reverso Context or the corpus at greek-language.gr — the word in twenty real sentences
Validate your own Greek. Search the exact phrase in quotes, ask a person, or post it where Greeks will correct it.

Keeping the spoken side alive.front: The specific risk of an input-heavy stage
Keeping the spoken side alive.back: C1 comprehension with A2 speech — and the gap becomes uncomfortable enough to avoid speaking, which widens it

Keeping the spoken side alive.front: Μπορούμε να μιλάμε μόνο ελληνικά; Θέλω να μάθω.
Keeping the spoken side alive.back: Can we speak only Greek? I want to learn. — the single most effective arrangement available
Correct me, please. — almost nobody says it, and it turns a polite conversation into a lesson
Can I help? — the opener that gets you into the work and the conversation
Ten minutes with a person. Not an hour, not a course. Weekly, for a year.

Keeping the spoken side alive.front: What Greeks make of a foreigner speaking Greek
Keeping the spoken side alive.back: Disproportionate pleasure — it is a small language nobody learns, so the effort reads as respect. Use the advantage.

Measuring progress honestly.back: Words known, cards reviewed, days on a streak, hours logged — all of them rise whether or not your Greek does
Pages per hour on known material; comprehension on one fixed recording; lookups per page; minutes without stopping; a written paragraph kept; a judgement on one spoken minute

Measuring progress honestly.front: Why a fixed benchmark recording works
Measuring progress honestly.back: The material is constant, so the change is you

Measuring progress honestly.front: The only comparison that contains information
Measuring progress honestly.back: Against your own March — not other learners, not natives, not the version of you who should be further along

A diagnostic: the Ellinomatheia paper.front: What Ellinomatheia is used for here
A diagnostic: the Ellinomatheia paper.back: A thermometer. The levels are the skeleton because they are an honest external description and the material is free — and no exam is ever taken.

A diagnostic: the Ellinomatheia paper.front: The five parts of an Ellinomatheia paper
A diagnostic: the Ellinomatheia paper.back: Reading comprehension; use of language; listening; written production; spoken production — and the first three mark themselves from the published keys

A diagnostic: the Ellinomatheia paper.front: What B2 means, in plain terms
A diagnostic: the Ellinomatheia paper.back: Arguing a position, following a discussion between natives, reading a newspaper, writing a structured text

A diagnostic: the Ellinomatheia paper.front: What C1 means, in plain terms
A diagnostic: the Ellinomatheia paper.back: Fluent and nearly effortless: implicit meaning, register control, literature

A diagnostic: the Ellinomatheia paper.front: The one thing not to do with a past paper
A diagnostic: the Ellinomatheia paper.back: Study for it. Practising papers raises your score and not your Greek, which defeats its only purpose here.

A diagnostic: the Ellinomatheia paper.front: Where the levels will be uneven, and it is normal
A diagnostic: the Ellinomatheia paper.back: Reading outruns writing by a level, and writing outruns speaking unless the ten minutes a week has been happening

A week of stage 8, written out.front: The daily non-negotiables, when the week collapses
A week of stage 8, written out.back: The daily saint (four minutes), the deck (ten), one retelling (thirty seconds). Fifteen minutes, and the chain holds.
Ten minutes of conversation, one journal entry, one intensive session, and some pages of a book so that books get finished

A week of stage 8, written out.front: The best-value day in the week
A week of stage 8, written out.back: Sunday — the service, the notices, the sermon, and the fifteen minutes before and after with the people

A week of stage 8, written out.front: What to cut first when the hour is not there
A week of stage 8, written out.back: The intensive work. Never the extensive.
Spelling and Forms run alongside and should finish inside it — two sessions a week, twenty minutes each

The long game.front: What changes at stage 8, in kind
The long game.back: Stages 1–7 were a course, finite and ordered. Stage 8 is the beginning of the permanent arrangement — a language you use rather than study.

The long game.front: Why the order was modern Greek first
The long game.back: Not pedagogy: the Greek people at church can teach you what the Liturgy means, and to be taught by them you have to be able to talk to them. The modern language buys you the teachers.

The long game.front: What stage 8 contributes to the classical curriculum
The long game.back: Several thousand words with ancient ancestors, the sound system, the case system, reading stamina, the Church’s modern vocabulary, and the people

The long game.front: The measure of this stage, in the end
The long game.back: Whether in five years there is Greek in your ordinary week without your having arranged it

Review: stage 8.back: Input at volume, with the method for each kind of material — and the practices that keep it running for years

Review: stage 8.front: The five checkpoint questions for stage 8
Review: stage 8.back: Have you finished a book in Greek? Is there unscheduled Greek in your week? Did the ten minutes of conversation happen most weeks? Are both tracks finished? Does the journal go back six months?

Review: stage 8.front: The one real task of stage 8
Review: stage 8.back: Finish a book in Greek. If that has not happened, stay here.
Not more comprehension — a reading habit that is already running, because you will write by imitating what you have read

What stage 9 is: producing Greek.front: Why writing comes after a stage of reading
What stage 9 is: producing Greek.back: You write by imitating what you have read. Before that you produce English sentences in Greek words.
Write what you can say — and never write a sentence whose shape you have not seen in Greek

What stage 9 is: producing Greek.front: Why writing is where you find out what you know
What stage 9 is: producing Greek.back: Speech is forgiving — gesture, hesitation, a helpful listener. Writing shows the spelling, the accents, the agreement and the register, and nothing moves on until you commit.

Handwriting at speed.back: After the word, as one movement at the end — placing it mid-word breaks the stroke and costs more than it saves

Handwriting at speed.front: The handwriting confusions to drill out
Handwriting at speed.back: ν against υ, θ against a barred ο, ζ against ξ, γ against ψ, μ against υ — and ς inside a word, which is a visible error

Handwriting at speed.front: The best combined drill in the curriculum
Handwriting at speed.back: Dictation — it tests listening, the i-spellings, the accents and the final -ν at once

Spelling under pressure.front: The single most useful fact about Greek spelling
Spelling under pressure.back: The endings are regular even when the roots are not — so most i decisions are grammar rather than memory
Kept on τον, την, δεν, μην, έναν before a vowel or a stop (κ π τ, μπ ντ γκ, τσ τζ, ξ ψ), dropped before other consonants — and when in doubt, keep it
Count the accents; ask of every i whether it is an ending; check final -ν; check the verb endings; check agreement; read it aloud

Spelling under pressure.front: Which i endings are decided by grammar
Spelling under pressure.back: -ει third person singular, -η feminine singular, -οι masculine plural, -ι neuter singular

Punctuation in full.back: A semicolon: ;  — and on the Greek keyboard it is the q key. Writing ? is a visible foreignism.
The raised dot · — Greek’s semicolon. alt gr + w on the standard layout.

Punctuation in full.front: Greek quotation marks, and the full stop
Punctuation in full.back: Guillemets « » — and the full stop goes OUTSIDE the closing mark
No comma before ότι, να or an indirect question — and a comma is REQUIRED around a vocative
He said: "I’ll come tomorrow." — guillemets, and the full stop outside
from work — από + τη, elided with an apostrophe
me too — and this one has NO apostrophe, because κι is its own form
A dash at the start of the line: — Πού ήσουν;

The sentence: from short to long.front: The five ways Greek extends a sentence
The sentence: from short to long.back: Coordination, subordination, a relative clause, a participle, and nominalisation

The sentence: from short to long.front: The most characteristic move of written Greek
The sentence: from short to long.back: Front-loading — a participle, an adverbial or a subordinate clause before the main verb arrives

The sentence: from short to long.front: The three ways a learner’s long sentence breaks
The sentence: from short to long.back: The verb never arrives; the agreement drifts across the distance; the participle has the wrong subject

The sentence: from short to long.front: Παρά τις δυσκολίες, και έχοντας υπόψη όσα είχαν συμβεί, η επιτροπή αποφάσισε να προχωρήσει.
The sentence: from short to long.back: Despite the difficulties, and bearing in mind what had happened, the committee decided to proceed. — front-loaded written Greek

The sentence: from short to long.front: Η απόφαση, η οποία ανακοινώθηκε χθες, άλλαξε τα πάντα.
The sentence: from short to long.back: The decision, which was announced yesterday, changed everything. — ο οποίος, the formal relative

The connective inventory.back: Commonly second or third in its clause, unlike English however: Δεν ήρθε όμως.
Do not over-signpost — one or two a paragraph; and match the register, because ως εκ τούτου in a message is absurd and λοιπόν in a formal letter is wrong

Paragraphs, and how a Greek text is orga.back: Four to eight sentences carrying one idea developed — longer than modern English journalism trains you to expect

Paragraphs, and how a Greek text is orga.front: The three parts of a Greek text
Paragraphs, and how a Greek text is orga.back: Πρόλογος, κύριο μέρος, επίλογος — and the conclusion is expected to state a position, not merely summarise
In recent years… — the standard Greek essay opening
In closing, I would say that…

Paragraphs, and how a Greek text is orga.front: How Greek expository prose moves between sentences
Paragraphs, and how a Greek text is orga.back: A clause is nominalised and the noun phrase becomes the next sentence’s subject

Register: the four levels.front: The four registers of written Greek
Register: the four levels.back: Intimate and online; everyday neutral; formal; learned and ecclesiastical — and level 4 is read, not written, except the clergy’s forms of address

Register: the four levels.front: The commonest learner error in written Greek
Register: the four levels.back: Mixing levels in one text. Pick a level before the first word and hold it to the end.
Neutral. Most of what you write is level 2, and over-formality reads as cold.
I state, I declare — the formal λέω
I carry out — the formal κάνω
I observe, I ascertain — the formal βλέπω
I would ask you to… — the polite conditional, formal register

The passive and the impersonal in writin.front: The main job of the written passive
The passive and the impersonal in writin.back: Hiding the agent. Official and journalistic Greek avoids naming who did a thing, and reading it means noticing the omission.
The suspension of operation was decided. — nobody is responsible in this sentence, and that is the point

The passive and the impersonal in writin.front: When NOT to use the passive
The passive and the impersonal in writin.back: When a human is doing something to another human. Σας ευχαριστώ — not Ευχαριστίες εκφράζονται.
The ordinary modern aorist passive against the learned form found in headlines, notices and church texts. Read both, write the first.

Nominalisation.front: What nominalisation is, and why Greek does it readily
Nominalisation.back: A clause becomes a noun phrase. Greek nouns decline, so the phrase slots into any role without rewriting the sentence — which English cannot do as neatly.

Nominalisation.front: The suffix that makes most abstract written vocabulary
Nominalisation.back: -ση / -ξη / -ψη, off the perfective stem: απόφαση, ανακοίνωση, αύξηση, λήψη, κατανόηση

Nominalisation.front: η ανακοίνωση της απόφασης της κυβέρνησης
Nominalisation.back: the announcement of the government’s decision — a genitive chain three deep, which is normal; four is bad writing even in Greek
the development, the course of events

Nominalisation.front: The nominalisation rule for your own writing
Nominalisation.back: One per sentence, and keep a real verb — three nominalisations and a weak verb is the nonsense of an official document

The participles in writing.front: What the active participle does in a text
The participles in writing.back: Replaces a whole subordinate clause in one word — Φτάνοντας, είδα… for Όταν έφτασα, είδα…
μη, not δεν: μη γνωρίζοντας, μη έχοντας

The participles in writing.front: The iron rule of the participle
The participles in writing.back: Its subject must be the main clause’s subject. Φτάνοντας στο σπίτι, η πόρτα ήταν ανοιχτή is wrong — the door did not arrive.

The participles in writing.front: Έχοντας ολοκληρώσει τις σπουδές του, επέστρεψε.
The participles in writing.back: Having completed his studies, he returned. — the compound participle, formal and useful
The short form is a state; the -μένος form implies someone did it. Same for ανοιχτός/ανοιγμένος, γεμάτος/γεμισμένος.
the interested party — a learned participle fully naturalised as a noun
the undersigned — learned, and live in official writing
the data — an ancient passive participle, now an ordinary noun

The participles in writing.front: How many participles a paragraph can take
The participles in writing.back: One well-placed one makes it read as written Greek. Three in a row make it unreadable.

The learned forms you cannot avoid.front: Why katharevousa survives in official and church Greek
The learned forms you cannot avoid.back: It was the official written language until 1976, so everything administrative, legal and ecclesiastical was written in it for a century and a half — and the forms survive where that writing is still copied

The learned forms you cannot avoid.front: The seven learned forms you SHOULD write
The learned forms you cannot avoid.back: ο οποίος; ο εν λόγω; the fixed datives (εν τω μεταξύ, εντάξει, δόξα τω Θεώ); εξ αρχής and εκ νέου; υπέρ and κατά + genitive; the formal verb set; and the clergy’s forms of address
in any case — a surviving dative
the aforementioned, the said — live in official writing
unconditionally — άνευ is the ancient preposition for without
in person, face to face — literally "through the living voice"

The learned forms you cannot avoid.front: Why not to write the rest of the learned register
The learned forms you cannot avoid.back: Producing a register you do not fully control makes you sound confused rather than learned — and it belongs to the later classical curriculum

Messages, and the internet's Greek.back: Greek written in Latin letters, from the days of phones without a Greek keyboard. Read it; do not write it.

Messages, and the internet's Greek.front: The one punctuation mark messaging keeps
Messages, and the internet's Greek.back: The question mark ; — because without it a question is not a question
Let me know when you can.
Little kisses — a light, warm sign-off

Messages, and the internet's Greek.front: Why you should keep the accents in messages even though Greeks drop them
Messages, and the internet's Greek.back: Your spelling study depends on them. Writing accent-free is a habit you cannot afford while you are still learning where they go.

An email.back: Good morning — the safe neutral email opening, right for nine emails in ten
Dear Sir / Madam — the formal, institutional opening
Yours sincerely — the formal default close
I remain at your disposal. — formal, and expected in business Greek

An email.front: The vocative trap in an email greeting
An email.back: Masculine -ος becomes -ε and -ης becomes -η: Αγαπητέ κύριε Παπαδόπουλε, Γιάννη, Νίκο. Feminines do not change.

An email.front: What goes in a Greek subject line
An email.back: A noun phrase, not a sentence: Αίτηση για βεβαίωση. Ερώτηση σχετικά με το ωράριο.

A formal letter.front: How a Greek letter is dated
A formal letter.back: Place first, then the day, then the month in the GENITIVE: Υόρκη, 14 Οκτωβρίου 2026

A formal letter.front: Με την παρούσα σας ενημερώνω ότι…
A formal letter.back: By the present letter I inform you that…

A formal letter.front: Παρακαλώ για τις δικές σας ενέργειες.
A formal letter.back: Please take the necessary action. — a standard and very useful formula

A formal letter.front: Είμαι στη διάθεσή σας για κάθε διευκρίνιση.
A formal letter.back: I am available for any clarification.
the letter (formal) — το γράμμα is a letter to a friend
competent, responsible — the right office for the matter
within (a period of time) — learned, and standard in a letter

A formal letter.front: Why not to write an angry letter in Greek
A formal letter.back: The formal register is the whole weapon. Adding heat weakens it, and a foreigner writing angry Greek is simply hard to read.

Forms, applications and officialdom.back: a sworn declaration — a fixture of Greek life, on a standard form
the reference number of a document
To be completed by the office
Please issue me a certificate… — the whole of a Greek application, in one sentence
the registry office — births, marriages and deaths
the diocesan office — where a baptismal or marriage certificate comes from

A notice, a programme, an announcement.front: The grammar of a Greek notice
A notice, a programme, an announcement.back: Nominal and nearly verbless: capitals in the heading (so no accents), genitives in the title, dates without the year, and one real verb if any
We inform you that… — the standard announcement opening

A notice, a programme, an announcement.front: Η παρουσία σας θα μας τιμήσει.
A notice, a programme, an announcement.back: Your presence will honour us. — the standard close of a Greek invitation
the patron saint of a town or parish
the patronal feast — colloquially το πανηγύρι

A notice, a programme, an announcement.front: Why a parish notice is formal in Greek
A notice, a programme, an announcement.back: Public writing in Greek is level 3 more consistently than in English. A chatty Greek notice reads as odd.

The CV and the covering letter.back: the CV — usually shortened to το βιογραφικό

The CV and the covering letter.front: How Greek states a language level on a CV
The CV and the covering letter.back: By certificate band: άριστη (C2), πολύ καλή (C1), καλή (B2), βασική γνώση. And χωρίς πιστοποίηση — uncertified — is an ordinary thing to write.

The CV and the covering letter.front: What a Greek CV includes that a British one does not
The CV and the covering letter.back: Date of birth, marital status, and military service for men — included without comment
I have experience in the field of…

The CV and the covering letter.front: Με ιδιαίτερο ενδιαφέρον διάβασα την αγγελία σας.
The CV and the covering letter.back: I read your advertisement with particular interest.
I meet the requirements of the post

The CV and the covering letter.front: Why to write your CV in Greek even if you never send it
The CV and the covering letter.back: It is the best self-description exercise there is — naming what you do, know and have done, which is the content of every conversation about yourself

Describing.back: is situated — the standard verb for placing something
at the edge of the village
He is one of those people who… — a very Greek frame
as if he were weighing every word — σαν να + the subjunctive

Describing.front: The tense for description in the past
Describing.back: The imperfect — states and habits. An aorist turns a description into a sequence of events.

Narrating.front: The division of labour in a Greek narrative
Narrating.back: Aorist for the events, one after another; imperfect for the background — weather, clothes, what was going on

Narrating.front: The historic present, and when Greeks use it
Narrating.back: A story told in the present for immediacy — extremely common in spoken narrative: Μπαίνω μέσα, και τι να δω;
And what do I see? — the fixed move for the surprise in a told story
He told me he would come. — NO tense shift in Greek reported speech

Narrating.front: How a told Greek story ends
Narrating.back: With a judgement rather than a stop: Από τότε δεν ξαναπήγα. Και κατάλαβα ότι… Έτσι είναι.

Narrating.front: The five parts of a narrative
Narrating.back: Setting and ordinary state in the imperfect; the breaking event in the aorist; what followed, in order; the outcome and what it meant

Explaining.back: it is a matter of…, this is a…
The gnomic present — things generally true, even if the thing happens annually
Each sentence starts from what the previous one established and adds one new thing — the most useful compositional habit in any language

Explaining.front: The person to avoid in an explanation
Explaining.back: The second person. Παίρνεις το αλεύρι… is recipe register. Use the impersonal passive.

Arguing: building a position.back: the disadvantage — πλεονέκτημα for the advantage

Arguing: building a position.front: The four moves of a body paragraph
Arguing: building a position.back: The claim; the reason (επειδή); the evidence or example; the link back to the thesis (συνεπώς)
Flat assertion reads as unpersuasive and is marked down. κατά τη γνώμη μου, σε μεγάλο βαθμό, φαίνεται ότι.

Arguing: conceding and refuting.back: It is true that…, however… — the most useful structure in argumentative writing

Arguing: conceding and refuting.front: Θα μπορούσε να αντιτείνει κανείς ότι…

Arguing: conceding and refuting.back: This argument overlooks that… — the workhorse refutation

Arguing: conceding and refuting.front: Θα ήταν υπερβολή να πούμε ότι…
Arguing: conceding and refuting.back: It would be an exaggeration to say that…

Arguing: conceding and refuting.front: The shape of a good concession
Arguing: conceding and refuting.back: Concede fully, then turn. A half-hearted concession is worse than none, because the reader sees it.

Arguing: conceding and refuting.front: The tone difference from British English
Arguing: conceding and refuting.back: Greek argument is more direct: Αυτό είναι λάθος is normal where British English would hedge. Over-hedging in Greek reads as evasive.

Summarising.front: The discipline that makes a summary a summary
Summarising.back: Write it from your marks with the original CLOSED. Writing with the text open produces paraphrase.

Summarising.front: The three rules of a summary
Summarising.back: No new information; no opinion; no copied sentences

Summarising.front: What learners keep that should go, and drop that should stay
Summarising.back: Drop the examples; keep the main claim stated AS a claim, and the structure of the argument

A review, and an opinion piece.back: Prompted by… — the standard opening of Greek opinion writing

A review, and an opinion piece.front: Το ερώτημα, τελικά, δεν είναι αν… αλλά αν…
A review, and an opinion piece.back: The question, in the end, is not whether… but whether… — the closing turn

A review, and an opinion piece.front: Why posting Greek in public is worth the exposure
A review, and an opinion piece.back: A corrected sentence is worth ten uncorrected ones, and Greeks correcting a foreigner are almost always pleased rather than scornful

Writing to the Church.back: Reverend Father — the formal letter opening to a parish priest
I ask your prayers. — the standard closing request, expected rather than presumptuous
I kiss your right hand. — the traditional close of a letter to a priest or bishop
Reverend Father — the simple formal opening of a letter to a priest
Your Eminence — the opening of a letter to a metropolitan
the archimandrite — a senior unmarried priest; addressed Πανοσιολογιώτατε in writing
the written address to a deacon — spoken, Διάκονε
Your Grace — to an auxiliary bishop
Your All-Holiness — to the Ecumenical Patriarch
to an archimandrite or an abbot
Mother — the address to an abbess; Γέροντα to an elder
a married priest's wife — and the address to her
I wish you strength. — for someone working or in a hard time
With the love of Christ — a warm close

Writing to the Church.front: Why the clergy’s forms are the one learned register to produce
Writing to the Church.back: They are formulae rather than a register to control, and getting them wrong is not informality but error

Writing to the Church.front: The -τατος pattern in the forms of address
Writing to the Church.back: The ancient superlative: Σεβασμιώτατος, Παναγιώτατος, Μακαριώτατος, Αιδεσιμότατος — and all become vocatives in -ε or -η when you address someone

Editing your own Greek.front: The rule that makes editing possible
Editing your own Greek.back: Leave it a day. You cannot see your own sentences an hour after writing them — and if there is no tomorrow, read it aloud.

Editing your own Greek.front: The first item on the editing checklist
Editing your own Greek.back: Read it aloud. Half your errors are audible: a wrong ending, a missing article, a clause with no verb.

Read aloud; one main verb present; agreement; case after prepositions; aspect in every past verb; participle subjects; the accents; the i spellings; final -ν; register held; connectives doing their job; cut a tenth

Editing your own Greek.front: The errors specific to an English speaker
Editing your own Greek.back: A missing article; a possessive adjective Greek does not have; an infinitive that does not exist; pronoun order; a subject pronoun in every sentence; English punctuation; and the calque
Pass one for sense, ignoring spelling entirely. Pass two for form, mechanically, without rereading for sense.

Getting corrected.back: It catches errors you know to look for. The errors that matter most are the ones you do not know are errors.
How would YOU say it? — ask this rather than "is this right?", which only ever gets you "yes, fine"
We don't say it like that. — the normal, blunt register of Greek help, and far more useful than politeness

Getting corrected.front: What to do with a correction
Getting corrected.back: Write both versions side by side; classify the error; card it if it is a pattern; and REUSE the corrected sentence within a week, or it is forgotten
One person at church who agrees to correct you; a language exchange; LangCorrect or Journaly; the learner forums; and a corpus search of the exact phrase

Getting corrected.front: What it means if most corrections are register errors and calques
Getting corrected.back: You are writing English in Greek — and the fix is more reading, not more study

Where you should be at the end of stage.front: The state of the four skills at the end of stage 9
Where you should be at the end of stage.back: Reading B2 going to C1, listening B2, writing B2 — and speaking entirely dependent on whether the ten minutes a week happened

Where you should be at the end of stage.front: What you should NOT expect to be able to do
Where you should be at the end of stage.back: Write literary Greek; produce the learned register; write without errors; write fast. The goal was method and your own error list.

Where you should be at the end of stage.front: The six checkpoint questions for stage 9
Where you should be at the end of stage.back: Is there a file of a dozen texts? Has a Greek corrected any of it? Can you write to a priest without looking up the forms? Did you write the argument with a concession? Can you name a text’s register at a glance? Are both tracks finished?
No correction by a Greek. Everything else in the stage you can do alone; writing without correction fossilises.

Review: stage 9.back: Producing Greek: the mechanics, the sentence, the register, the practical texts, the four modes, and the discipline of editing and being corrected

Review: stage 9.front: The rule of the whole stage
Review: stage 9.back: Write what you can say, and delete any sentence whose shape you have not seen in Greek — replacing it with two simpler ones you know are right
Cyprus, and Literature and ad astra — neither gating the other, both on top of stage 8’s reading, which should by now be a habit

Review: stage 9.front: When the classical curriculum can begin
Review: stage 9.back: Whenever you want it. Nothing gates it, and everything from here is addition rather than progression.

What stage 10 is, and why Cyprus.front: Why Cypriot gets a stage in this curriculum
What stage 10 is, and why Cyprus.back: His ruling — standard AND Cypriot — and the fact that the Greek community in Britain is substantially Cypriot, so the parish hall may be speaking it
Understand the dialect; speak the standard. A foreigner speaking Cypriot reads as imitation, and every Cypriot speaks standard Greek anyway.
The dialect at home, with friends, in the village, in jokes and in anger; standard Greek in school, writing, news, church and public speech — sliding between them sentence by sentence

The sounds of Cypriot.front: The five sound differences of Cypriot
The sounds of Cypriot.back: Long double consonants; aspirated ππ/ττ/κκ; κ→τζ before ε and ι; χ→sh before ε and ι; and final -ν kept

The sounds of Cypriot.front: Why Cypriot sounds older than standard Greek
The sounds of Cypriot.back: Because it is — the long consonants, the final -ν and the post-verbal pronoun are all Ancient Greek retentions the standard dropped
και — the commonest word in the dialect, written τζαι, τζιαι, τσαι or τσιαι
χέρι — the hand, with the sh sound standard Greek has not got
τι καιρό κάνει; — What's the weather doing?
δεν βλέπω τίποτα — I can't see anything.

The sounds of Cypriot.front: Why Cypriot stops sound more familiar to an English ear
The sounds of Cypriot.back: The double voiceless stops are aspirated, as in English pot, top, cat — where standard Greek stops are unaspirated

Writing Cypriot: there is no standard sp.front: Why Cypriot has no standard orthography
Writing Cypriot: there is no standard sp.back: It has never been an official written language — standard Greek is what is taught, printed and used in church and government in Cyprus. The dialect is written anyway, by improvisation.

Writing Cypriot: there is no standard sp.front: The three systems for writing Cypriot
Writing Cypriot: there is no standard sp.back: Ordinary improvised spelling; the linguists' carons (σ̌, ζ̌, τσ̌, τζ̌); and Cypriot Greeklish with sh and j

Writing Cypriot: there is no standard sp.front: What to do with an unknown Cypriot word
Writing Cypriot: there is no standard sp.back: Apply the five sound rules in reverse first. If it yields a standard word you are done; if not, it is real dialect vocabulary or a loanword.

Writing Cypriot: there is no standard sp.front: What NOT to card from Cypriot
Writing Cypriot: there is no standard sp.back: The spellings. Card the word and the meaning, because the same word appears four ways.
the standard dialect dictionary — Λεξικό της Κυπριακής Διαλέκτου

The grammar: pronouns and negation.front: The biggest grammatical difference in Cypriot
The grammar: pronouns and negation.back: The weak pronoun FOLLOWS the verb: λαλώ σου, θωρώ σε, είπεν μου, ξέρω το — the older Greek order, which the standard keeps only in the imperative
είναι and δεν. A following verb means not; a following adjective, noun or adverb means is. Εν εν καλόν = it isn’t good.
εννά (also έννα) for θα — from θέλω να, as θα is. Standard θα is used in Cyprus too.
από πού — from where. Ancient Greek, unchanged, and ordinary speech in Cyprus.
λέω — I say. One of the three Cypriot verbs you must know.
είπε — with the final -ν kept; and έδωκεν for έδωσε
θα σου πω — I’ll tell you.
τι λες, κορίτσι μου; — What are you saying, girl?

The vocabulary that is genuinely differe.back: μιλώ, συνομιλώ — I talk, I converse
η καρέκλα — the chair, from Romance
το αγόρι, το παιδί — the boy, the child; κοπελλούι for the little one
girl — and used as an affectionate address to ANY woman, by men and women alike. No standard equivalent.
ο πατέρας — father, in dialect; and τζυρά for madam
Pascha, Easter — from λαμπρός, bright. The ordinary Cypriot word.
πιάνω, παίρνω — I take, I catch

The vocabulary that is genuinely differe.front: The Cypriot πολλά, and the confusion it causes
The vocabulary that is genuinely differe.back: In Cypriot it means VERY, where standard Greek uses πολύ. Εν πολλά καλόν = it’s very good.

The vocabulary that is genuinely differe.front: How to learn the Cypriot vocabulary
The vocabulary that is genuinely differe.back: Not as a list. Listen, and when a word does not resolve by the sound rules, look it up and card it — thirty or forty cover most ordinary speech.

The four foreign layers.front: The four foreign layers in Cypriot, in order
The four foreign layers.back: Old French (Lusignan, 1192–1489), Venetian Italian (1489–1571), Ottoman Turkish (1571–1878), English (1878 onwards) — over an Ancient Greek substrate
Commandaria — the sweet wine named for the Knights Hospitaller’s Grand Commandery
I manage, I command — from Italian comandare
the village headman — a Turkish-derived title still in use
full — English, and used as an intensifier meaning completely

The four foreign layers.front: Why a Turkish loanword does not mark a word as Cypriot
The four foreign layers.back: Standard Greek has hundreds too — καφές, γιαούρτι, κέφι, μεζές. Cypriot simply has more, and keeps some the mainland replaced.

The four foreign layers.front: The sensitivity about Turkish loanwords in Cypriot
The four foreign layers.back: Given 1974, do not make a thing of it. Linguists discuss it freely; it is not small talk.

The four foreign layers.front: Which layer to guess from a word’s subject
The four foreign layers.back: Food, probably Turkish; household, legal or building, Italian or French; cars, shops and offices, English

Food and the table in Cyprus.back: halloumi — grilled, fried or raw; traditionally sheep’s and goat’s milk, with mint between the folds
anari — the fresh whey cheese, like ricotta
stuffed vine leaves — mainland Greek calls them ντολμαδάκια
taro root, braised with pork or chicken — a Cypriot staple with no mainland equivalent
large pieces of meat on a long skewer over coals — NOT souvlaki, which is the small version
the Cypriot sausage in caul fat
pork in red wine and coriander seed
the Easter cheese pastries — made in Holy Week with cheese, eggs, mint and raisins, eaten the moment the fast breaks
black-eyed beans, boiled and dressed with lemon and oil
trachanas — cracked wheat soured with yoghurt, dried, made into soup
It's very tasty! — with the Cypriot πολλά

Food and the table in Cyprus.front: What a Cypriot μεζέ actually is
Food and the table in Cyprus.back: Twenty or thirty small dishes over two or three hours, ending with the grilled meat. Pacing yourself early is the only strategy.

Greetings and the Cypriot manner.back: τι κάνεις; — the Cypriot "how are you", and the one to recognise first
Welcome — said by the host about the arriving person, in the third person; the guest replies Καλώς σας βρήκα
to a craftsman, and to any man whose name you do not know
Where are you from? — and for a Cypriot the honest answer is a VILLAGE, even for someone born in London
Cypriot sociability runs on teasing — your accent, your age, your appetite. Being teased is being included; tease back or laugh, never explain yourself.

Greetings and the Cypriot manner.front: What to say when a Cypriot calls their own Greek "not proper Greek"
Greetings and the Cypriot manner.back: That it is proper Greek, and older than Athenian in several features. The apology comes from a century of being told otherwise.

The Church of Cyprus.front: When the Church of Cyprus became autocephalous
The Church of Cyprus.back: 431, at the Council of Ephesus — one of the oldest autocephalous Churches in Orthodoxy, older than the national Churches by a millennium and a half

The Church of Cyprus.front: The three privileges of the Archbishop of Cyprus
The Church of Cyprus.back: He signs in red ink, carries an imperial sceptre instead of a pastoral staff, and wears a purple mantle — granted by tradition by the Emperor Zeno
the Apostle Barnabas — a Cypriot from Salamis, the island’s apostle and the founder of its Church
Lazarus, raised by Christ, by tradition bishop of Kition — and his church stands in Larnaca
Saint Mamas, the shepherd saint with the lion — hugely popular in Cyprus
the twelfth-century hermit whose carved cave-monastery is near Paphos
Kykkos — the greatest Cypriot monastery, with an icon of the Mother of God attributed by tradition to Saint Luke, kept veiled
Stavrovouni — founded by tradition by Saint Helen, with a relic of the Cross
the monastery on the tip of the Karpas peninsula — in the occupied north, and a pilgrimage interrupted for decades
the Ethnarch — the Archbishop as civil head of the Orthodox population under Ottoman rule, which is why Makarios III became the first President
the Holy Saturday bonfire in Cyprus
the Pentecost Monday festival by the sea — flowers and water, over an older layer

The Church of Cyprus.front: Why the Church matters more in Cyprus than in Greece
The Church of Cyprus.back: It was the nation’s administration for three centuries under Ottoman rule, and the Archbishop was Ethnarch — so it is far more entangled with national identity

Cypriot history, in brief.front: How long Cyprus has been Greek-speaking
Cypriot history, in brief.back: Over three thousand years, from Mycenaean settlement around 1200 BC — the longest continuous Greek presence anywhere outside Greece
Richard I takes the island on the Third Crusade and sells it; the Lusignan kingdom follows, then Venice in 1489 and the Ottomans in 1571
British administration begins, leased from the Ottomans; annexed 1914, a Crown Colony from 1925, independent 1960
1955–59, against British rule, for enosis — union with Greece. It ended in independence rather than union.
Independence: the Republic of Cyprus, Makarios III as President, and two British Sovereign Base Areas retained

Cypriot history, in brief.front: Why there are Cypriots in Britain
Cypriot history, in brief.back: Migration from the 1930s, heavy through the 1950s and 60s, and a surge after 1974 — around 300,000 people of Cypriot descent, who built most of the Greek Orthodox parishes here
Archbishop, Ethnarch and first President — the dominant figure of twentieth-century Cyprus, and genuinely divisive. Do not have a view.

1974, and what not to say.back: The Greek junta backed a coup against Makarios; Turkey invaded five days later and took about 37 per cent of the island. Roughly 160,000 Greek Cypriots and 50,000 Turkish Cypriots were displaced, and some 2,000 people went missing.
the occupied territories — the standard Greek Cypriot term for the north
the missing — still being identified as graves are excavated
the Cyprus problem — the standard shorthand for the whole question
the enclaved — those who stayed in the north
"I do not forget" — taught to Cypriot schoolchildren since 1974, and closer to a vow than a slogan

1974, and what not to say.front: Ο Θεός να βάλει το χέρι του.
1974, and what not to say.back: May God put His hand to it. — expresses sympathy, hope and helplessness together, in the Church’s register, and commits to nothing

1974, and what not to say.front: The six things not to say about 1974
1974, and what not to say.back: Nothing a Turkish official would say; no proposed solution; no apportioning of blame; never that it was long ago; do not ask whether they have been back; and do not generalise about Turks — Turkish Cypriots and mainland Turkey are kept distinct

1974, and what not to say.front: What a newcomer should do when 1974 comes up
1974, and what not to say.back: Listen. Ask one question and hear the whole answer. Being the person who listened well is worth more than any opinion.

The diaspora: Cypriot Greek in Britain.front: The five features of British Cypriot Greek
The diaspora: Cypriot Greek in Britain.back: Code-switching mid-sentence; English loans with Greek endings (παρκάρω, σοπάρω); a frozen 1960s village vocabulary; English intonation in the young; and often no literacy in Greek
I park — an English loan naturalised with a Greek ending, like σοπάρω and ντραϊβάρω

The diaspora: Cypriot Greek in Britain.front: The inversion you should expect in a British parish
The diaspora: Cypriot Greek in Britain.back: You can read better than many fluent speakers, and they can speak better than you will for years. Both facts are ordinary.

The diaspora: Cypriot Greek in Britain.front: The best local Greek practice available to you
The diaspora: Cypriot Greek in Britain.back: The parish Greek school — most parishes run one, they teach standard Greek, and they are chronically short of help

The diaspora: Cypriot Greek in Britain.front: Είναι κανονικά ελληνικά, και πιο παλιά από τα αθηναϊκά.
The diaspora: Cypriot Greek in Britain.back: It is proper Greek, and older than Athenian. — true, and a genuine kindness to say

Cypriot music.back: the improvised rhyming couplet duels — two singers trading fifteen-syllable verses, each capping the last. UNESCO intangible heritage, and nothing comparable exists in mainland Greek music.
the traditional Cypriot melodic patterns on which singers improvise words — η φωνή της Μεσαρκάς, της Πάφου
the lute, which plays with the violin in Cypriot folk music
the best-known Cypriot singer-songwriter — clear diction, mostly standard Greek, widely loved in Greece too
the leading figure in preserving and performing the Cypriot traditional repertoire

Cypriot music.front: Why a traditional Cypriot song is harder than Cypriot speech
Cypriot music.back: Folk lyrics use the oldest, densest village vocabulary, archaic even in Cyprus — treat the obscure words as scenery

Dialect poetry: Michaelides and Lipertis.back: the national poet of Cyprus (1849–1917), who made the dialect a literary language
Michaelides’ great poem, on the execution of Archbishop Kyprianos and the bishops in 1821 — the central text of Cypriot literature, in dialect and in the fifteen-syllable folk metre
the other pillar of Cypriot dialect poetry (1866–1937) — Κυπριακά Τραγούδια, lyric, domestic, much of it set to music
a major modern Cypriot poet — his Στιγμές are two or three lines each, and the best way in for a learner
the leading contemporary Cypriot poet, in standard Greek, much of it about 1974

Dialect poetry: Michaelides and Lipertis.front: How to read dialect verse as a learner
Dialect poetry: Michaelides and Lipertis.back: Aloud, for the metre and the rhyme, before any glossary — then one pass with a gloss, then aloud again

Cypriot humour, and the sitcoms.front: Why a Cypriot sitcom is the best material in this stage
Cypriot humour, and the sitcoms.back: Dialect at natural speed, with the situation visible, and subtitled in standard Greek for Greek broadcast — a dialect-to-standard parallel text with audio
the long-running Cypriot village sitcom — dialect so broad that mainland Greeks need the subtitles, which means you get them too
the Cypriot sketch series — satirical and fast

Cypriot humour, and the sitcoms.front: The seven subjects of Cypriot humour
Cypriot humour, and the sitcoms.back: Village against town; the dialect itself; bureaucracy; family obligation; hospitality as warfare; the returning diaspora cousin; and mainland Greeks

Cypriot humour, and the sitcoms.front: The one joke not to join in on
Cypriot humour, and the sitcoms.back: Jokes about the dialect. Cypriots make them constantly; they are for its speakers to make.

Where to find Cypriot.back: the Cyprus Broadcasting Corporation — news in standard Greek, drama and comedy in dialect, and a large free archive

Where to find Cypriot.front: The one priority if you do only one thing in this stage
Where to find Cypriot.back: Watch a Cypriot sitcom with the Greek subtitles on, regularly — the only resource that gives dialect, standard, audio and context at once

Where to find Cypriot.front: Why this stage has no course
Where to find Cypriot.back: Cypriot has no graded readers, no comprehensible-input channel and no course that teaches it as a target. The sound rules and the vocabulary lessons substitute for one.

Where to find Cypriot.front: The resource that is on no list
Where to find Cypriot.back: The Cypriots at your church. Nothing online will teach you the particular Greek of the particular village your parish came from.

The island itself: places and names.back: Nicosia — the capital, and the last divided capital in Europe
Limassol — the biggest port and the commercial centre
Larnaca — the main airport, and Saint Lazarus’s city
Famagusta — in the occupied area; Βαρώσι is the sealed quarter
Kyrenia — occupied; the north coast and the castle
Morphou — occupied, and its feast of Saint Mamas is a byword
the Troodos range — the painted churches, the villages, and snow
the Kyrenia range — "the five fingers", occupied
the long north-eastern peninsula, with Apostolos Andreas at its tip
the central plain — the island’s granary, now largely occupied
το χωριό — the village, in dialect; the unit of Cypriot identity

The island itself: places and names.front: Which three city names to be careful with
The island itself: places and names.back: Famagusta, Kyrenia and Morphou — they are in the occupied north and they are the names on the Δεν ξεχνώ posters. Use the Greek names.

The island itself: places and names.front: The geographical fact that explains Cyprus
The island itself: places and names.back: It is closer to Syria and Lebanon than to Greece — which has shaped its food, its loanwords, its history and its politics

Speaking with Cypriots.front: The three reasons not to speak the dialect
Speaking with Cypriots.back: It reads as imitation of a dialect its speakers have been mocked for; you will get it wrong in ways that are funny rather than endearing; and every Cypriot speaks standard Greek anyway

Speaking with Cypriots.front: Πώς θα το έλεγε ένας Ελλαδίτης;
Speaking with Cypriots.back: How would someone from Greece say it? — the right way to ask for the standard equivalent, because it treats both as equal

Speaking with Cypriots.front: The phrase to avoid when asking about dialect
Speaking with Cypriots.back: "στα κανονικά" — "in proper Greek". The word proper is the loaded one.

Speaking with Cypriots.front: What dialect may enter your own speech, and what may not
Speaking with Cypriots.back: Adopt what is said to you repeatedly — κουμπάρε, Να ’στε καλά, the food words, η Λαμπρή. Import nothing you have only read.

Speaking with Cypriots.front: The four things never to do with a Cypriot’s Greek
Speaking with Cypriots.back: Do not correct it; do not call it village Greek; do not perform the dialect as a joke; and do not treat it as a lesser Greek

Speaking with Cypriots.front: The best question available in a Cypriot parish
Speaking with Cypriots.back: Which village their family came from. It never fails.

Where you should be at the end of stage.front: The six checkpoint questions for stage 10
Where you should be at the end of stage.back: Can you convert ten Cypriot words by the sound rules? Do you recognise εν, εννά and the post-verbal pronoun instantly? Have you watched a sitcom and written an exchange both ways? Do you know the four words of 1974? Have you asked about someone’s village? Do you know three words your parish uses that no book has?
The percentage of parish-hall conversation you follow — measured with a clip at the start and at the end

Where you should be at the end of stage.front: How Cypriot prepares you for the classical curriculum
Where you should be at the end of stage.back: The long consonants, the final -ν, the post-verbal pronoun and πόθεν are all Ancient Greek, kept in Cyprus and lost in Athens — so hearing them is hearing older Greek

Review: stage 10.back: The five sound rules, the four grammatical differences, the core vocabulary, the four loanword layers, the Church and history of the island, and the people in the hall

Review: stage 10.front: What this stage was actually about
Review: stage 10.back: Not a dialect in the abstract. Following the conversation, because the Greeks at the parish are more likely to be Cypriot than Greek.

What stage 11 is: no more course.front: Why literature is the end of the route, not the middle
What stage 11 is: no more course.back: It is the hardest Greek — the full historical depth of the language, used deliberately; it requires everything else first; and it is the point. The rest was infrastructure.
Maps, not instruction: what a body of work is, why it matters, how hard it is, where to find it free, and which piece to start with

What stage 11 is: no more course.front: Why stage 11 is the threshold of the classical curriculum
What stage 11 is: no more course.back: Papadiamantis, Kontoglou, the theologians and the hymnographers all write in or towards the learned register — the point at which modern Greek has taken you as far as it can

How to read a Greek poem.back: the fifteen-syllable line — iambic, with a break after the eighth syllable. The Greek line: the folk songs, the Erotokritos, Solomos, and much verse that looks free.

How to read a Greek poem.front: The central technique of Greek poetry since the nineteenth century
How to read a Greek poem.back: The register shift — a learned word in a demotic line, or an ancient form, where the shift itself carries the irony, distance or grandeur

How to read a Greek poem.front: The six steps for reading a Greek poem
How to read a Greek poem.back: Aloud whole; aloud for the metre; for sense; marking the register shifts; aloud again; and four lines by heart

How to read a Greek poem.front: Why to learn four lines of a poem by heart
How to read a Greek poem.back: A poem memorised is in your Greek permanently, and Greeks quote poetry in ordinary conversation — having four lines is a form of membership

Cavafy.front: Why Cavafy is the way into Greek poetry for a learner
Cavafy.back: Short poems, plain vocabulary, prosaic syntax and concrete situations — and 154 canonical poems in all
His Greek mixes demotic with katharevousa and with the Greek of Alexandria and the Phanar, and the mixture IS the poem

Cavafy.front: Να εύχεσαι να ’ναι μακρύς ο δρόμος.
Cavafy.back: Pray that the road is long. — Ithaca

Cavafy.front: Δεν θα βρεις άλλη γη, δεν θα βρεις άλλη θάλασσα. Η πόλις θα σε ακολουθεί.
Cavafy.back: You will find no new lands, no other seas. The city will follow you. — Η Πόλις
Cavafy’s most quoted poem — the journey rather than the arrival; said at graduations, retirements and funerals
Waiting for the Barbarians — a city that needs its enemy
The God Abandons Antony — on losing with dignity
A learned accusative plural where demotic would have λιμάνια — the archaism lifts the harbours into myth. Cavafy in one word.

Seferis.back: Γιώργος Σεφέρης, 1900–1971; born in Smyrna and driven out as a boy; career diplomat; the first Greek Nobel, 1963; denounced the junta publicly in 1969

Seferis.front: Όπου και να ταξιδέψω η Ελλάδα με πληγώνει.
Seferis.back: Wherever I travel, Greece wounds me.

Seferis.front: Ξύπνησα με το μαρμάρινο τούτο κεφάλι στα χέρια
Seferis.back: I woke with this marble head in my hands — Μυθιστόρημα III, and the most quoted image in modern Greek poetry about the classical inheritance
Seferis’ central work, 1935: twenty-four poems, free verse, the Argonauts as the century’s refugees
Seferis’ Cyprus book, from his 1953 visit — originally titled «Κύπρον, ου μ’ εθέσπισεν…», and the right reading after stage 10
Seferis’ essays — lucid prose, and his piece on Cavafy teaches more than any introduction

Elytis.back: Οδυσσέας Ελύτης, 1911–1996; born in Heraklion to a Lesvos family; fought in the Albanian campaign; Nobel 1979. The name is assembled from Ελλάδα, ελπίδα, ελευθερία, Ελένη.

Elytis.front: Τη γλώσσα μου έδωσαν ελληνική· το σπίτι φτωχικό στις αμμουδιές του Ομήρου.
Elytis.back: They gave me the Greek language; a poor house on Homer’s shores. — the most quoted statement in modern Greek about the Greek language

Elytis.front: Ένα το χελιδόνι και η άνοιξη ακριβή, για να γυρίσει ο ήλιος θέλει δουλειά πολλή.
Elytis.back: One swallow, and spring is dear; for the sun to turn takes much work.
Elytis’ central work, 1959 — in three parts (Γένεσις, Πάθη, Δοξαστικόν), built on the shape of an Orthodox office, and set by Theodorakis in 1964

Elytis.front: Where the title Άξιον Εστί comes from
Elytis.back: The hymn to the Mother of God in the Divine Liturgy — "it is meet and right". Elytis built the sequence as a service: a Genesis, a Passion and a Doxology.

Ritsos, and the poems that became songs.back: Γιάννης Ρίτσος, 1909–1990; tuberculosis, the resistance, and exile on Makronisos, Ai Stratis and Leros; more than a hundred volumes; never given the Nobel, which Greeks still mention
Ritsos, 1936 — a mother’s lament over her son, shot in the Thessaloniki tobacco strike. In the folk fifteen-syllable, publicly burned by the Metaxas dictatorship, and set by Theodorakis in 1958.

Ritsos, and the poems that became songs.front: Γιε μου, σπλάχνο των σπλάχνων μου, καρδούλα της καρδιάς μου
Ritsos, and the poems that became songs.back: My son, flesh of my flesh, little heart of my heart — the opening of Επιτάφιος, in the register of the Greek funeral lament

Ritsos, and the poems that became songs.front: What Ritsos did in Επιτάφιος that every Greek hears
Ritsos, and the poems that became songs.back: He wrote a mother’s lament in the form of the Church’s own Εγκώμια, the Lamentations of Holy Friday — an atheist and a communist using the Church’s language because there is nothing else to use
Ritsos, 1973 — eighteen short songs of the bitter homeland, written under the junta and set by Theodorakis
Hadjidakis, 1972 — Sappho, the Song of Songs, Erotokritos, Solomos, Cavafy, Elytis and Seferis on one record. A complete anthology of Greek love poetry with audio.
On the hidden shore — Theodorakis setting Seferis’ Άρνηση; everybody sings it, and most people do not know it is Seferis

Solomos, Palamas and the nineteenth cent.front: Μήγαρις έχω άλλο στο νου μου πάρεξ ελευθερία και γλώσσα;
Solomos, Palamas and the nineteenth cent.back: Have I anything else in my mind but freedom and language? — Solomos, and the foundation of modern Greek literature

Solomos, Palamas and the nineteenth cent.front: Σε γνωρίζω από την κόψη του σπαθιού την τρομερή
Solomos, Palamas and the nineteenth cent.back: I know you by the terrible edge of your sword — the first line of the national anthem of Greece AND of Cyprus, from Solomos’ Ύμνος εις την Ελευθερίαν

Solomos, Palamas and the nineteenth cent.front: Solomos’ decision, and why it founds everything after him
Solomos, Palamas and the nineteenth cent.back: He turned deliberately to the demotic at a moment when educated opinion held that serious literature required the learned language

Solomos, Palamas and the nineteenth cent.front: The thing to know about Solomos’ work
Solomos, Palamas and the nineteenth cent.back: Almost all of it is a fragment. He revised obsessively and finished little; what survives was assembled by editors.
Solomos’ greatest poem — a shipwrecked Cretan, his dying beloved, and a vision. A fragment.
the dominant Greek literary figure of the generation after Solomos (1859–1943) — Ο Δωδεκάλογος του Γύφτου, Η Φλογέρα του Βασιλιά, and Ο Τάφος
It became a national demonstration under German occupation: thousands followed the coffin, Sikelianos read over the grave, and the crowd sang the national anthem in front of the occupying troops
the other Zakynthian (1792–1869) — twenty odes in an archaising Pindaric Greek. Admired more than read.

The folk song, and Crete.back: the demotic song — centuries of anonymous oral poetry in the fifteen-syllable line, and the acknowledged foundation of modern Greek literary language
the Akritic songs — the Byzantine frontier guards, and Digenis wrestling with Death. The oldest layer.
the ballads — narrative, supernatural, often terrible
the laments — and in Mani a formal art with named composers
The Dead Brother — Constantine rises from the grave to fetch his sister home. Pan-Balkan, and the Greek version the richest.
The Bridge of Arta — the master builder’s wife walled in to make the bridge stand. The most famous Greek folk ballad.

The folk song, and Crete.front: Ολημερίς το χτίζανε, το βράδυ εγκρεμιζόταν.
The folk song, and Crete.back: All day they built it, and at evening it fell down. — Της Άρτας το γιοφύρι
Kornaros, c. 1600 — 10,000 lines of rhymed fifteen-syllable Cretan verse, still sung in Crete to the lyra

The folk song, and Crete.front: Του Κύκλου τα γυρίσματα, που ανεβοκατεβαίνου
The folk song, and Crete.back: The turnings of the Wheel, that rise and fall — the opening of the Erotokritos
The Sacrifice of Abraham — the Cretan religious drama

The folk song, and Crete.front: What Cretan and Cypriot have in common
The folk song, and Crete.back: The two great surviving Greek dialects with literatures of their own: ancient features kept, a fifteen-syllable tradition, and improvised verse contests — Cretan μαντινάδες and Cypriot τσιαττιστά

Papadiamantis.back: Αλέξανδρος Παπαδιαμάντης, 1851–1911; son of a priest from Skiathos; lived in poverty in Athens; WAS A CHANTER, singing Byzantine chant at Saint Elisseos for decades. Two hundred stories, and held to be the greatest Greek prose writer.

Papadiamantis.front: Why Papadiamantis is the hardest prose in the curriculum
Papadiamantis.back: Narration in katharevousa, dialogue in the Skiathos dialect, liturgical and scriptural quotation in Koine woven in unmarked, and long periodic sentences

Papadiamantis.front: Why Papadiamantis matters most for this curriculum’s purpose
Papadiamantis.back: No writer in the language is closer to the Church: the parish, the feasts, the fasts, the chanting, the priest, the poor widow and the sea, written from inside the liturgical year
The Murderess, 1903 — an old woman on Skiathos who drowns infant girls out of a terrible compassion. His masterpiece, about a hundred pages.
the Christmas story — a village walking through snow to the fortress church to keep the feast. The Orthodox Christmas in a short story, and where to start.
A Dream on the Wave — the shepherd boy, Moschoula and the sea. The most anthologised Greek short story.

Papadiamantis.front: Ήμουν πτωχόν παιδίον, βοσκόπουλο εις τα όρη…
Papadiamantis.back: I was a poor child, a shepherd boy in the mountains — three katharevousa forms in eight words: πτωχόν, παιδίον, εις

Papadiamantis.front: Why both the Church and Greek literature claim Papadiamantis
Papadiamantis.back: He is the bridge: the writer modern Greek Orthodox writers measure themselves against, and at the same time the consensus choice as the language’s finest prose stylist

Kazantzakis.front: Why Kazantzakis is harder in Greek than in translation
Kazantzakis.back: An enormous vocabulary of Cretan dialect, village words and his own coinages, long rolling sentences borrowed from the folk song, and militant demotic pushed to its limits
Report to Greco — the autobiography addressed to El Greco. The most beautiful and the most readable; where a learner should start.
Christ Recrucified, 1948 — a village passion play and the refugees who arrive during it. By many judgements his best novel.
The Saviours of God, 1927 — the metaphysical credo, and the key to all the rest

No. The Holy Synod of the Church of Greece considered action in 1955 over The Last Temptation and did not excommunicate him; the widely repeated claim is false. The Roman Catholic Church put the book on the Index.

Kazantzakis.front: Δεν ελπίζω τίποτα. Δε φοβούμαι τίποτα. Είμαι λέφτερος.
Kazantzakis.back: I hope for nothing. I fear nothing. I am free. — his epitaph, cut into the Martinengo bastion in Heraklion

Kazantzakis.front: How to read Kazantzakis as an Orthodox reader
Kazantzakis.back: Not as an Orthodox writer, and as one unavoidably formed by Orthodoxy — his lifelong subject is an ascetic’s subject, handled by a man who would not submit to the ascesis

The Generation of the Thirties, and Asia.front: What the Generation of the Thirties set out to do
The Generation of the Thirties, and Asia.back: Make a modern Greek literature both European and Greek — Seferis and Elytis in poetry, Myrivilis, Venezis, Theotokas, Karagatsis and Prevelakis in prose. Their programme was Ελληνικότητα.

The Generation of the Thirties, and Asia.front: The Asia Minor Catastrophe, in figures
The Generation of the Thirties, and Asia.back: In 1922 the Greek advance into Anatolia collapsed and Smyrna burned; by the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne roughly 1.2 million Orthodox Christians were expelled to Greece and about 400,000 Muslims to Turkey. Greece’s population rose by a quarter.
the uprooting — the Greek word for the whole 1922 event, and used of Cyprus in 1974 too
the lost homelands — Asia Minor, Pontus, Eastern Thrace
Dido Sotiriou, 1962 — the Asia Minor novel most Greeks have read, narrated plainly by a villager. The readable way in.
Stratis Doukas, 1929 — forty pages in the voice of the man who lived it, and as clean a piece of Greek prose as exists
Myrivilis, 1924 — Life in the Tomb, the Macedonian front in letters. The great Greek war book, and hard.
Venezis, 1931 — the author’s own experience in the Turkish labour battalions

The Generation of the Thirties, and Asia.front: The three displacements that made the Greek diaspora in Britain
The Generation of the Thirties, and Asia.back: 1922 from Asia Minor, the post-war emigration from Greece and Cyprus, and 1974 from northern Cyprus

The civil war, and the post-war novel.back: the Civil War, 1946–49 — and the word alone is enough
the Occupation, 1941–44 — German, Italian and Bulgarian, with mass starvation in Athens in the winter of 1941–42
the Polytechnic — 17 November 1973, the student rising against the junta, and a national holiday
the barren prison islands — Makronisos, Ai Stratis, Gyaros
Tachtsis, 1962 — two women talking across forty years of Greek history, in the most natural spoken Greek in any Greek novel. The best book in this stage for a learner.
Alexandrou, 1974 — the great novel of the Greek left’s self-destruction: a man writing his defence about a box that turns out to be empty
short autobiographical prose about Thessaloniki, the occupation and the refugee quarters — plain modern Greek, beautiful, and attentive to the feasts

The civil war, and the post-war novel.front: The social rule about the civil war, as about 1974
The civil war, and the post-war novel.back: Do not take a side. The division is live in politics and in families, and a foreigner’s opinion about EAM or the colonels is not wanted.

The civil war, and the post-war novel.front: The Church’s own position in this history
The civil war, and the post-war novel.back: Contested: Archbishop Damaskinos and the rescue of Athenian Jews on one side of the ledger, accommodations with the colonels on another. Know that it is contested; do not adjudicate it.

Contemporary Greek writing.back: Christos Oikonomou — sixteen stories from the Piraeus of the crisis, in stripped-down Greek. For many readers the best Greek prose of the last twenty years.
the most loved Greek poet of recent decades (1931–2020) — ordinary vocabulary used strangely, grief, and grammatical terms turned into images. Accessible to a learner.
a free online Greek literary monthly — poetry, prose and essays, current. The best single free source for contemporary writing.
the free online Greek literary review — reviews of everything as it appears
Και με το φως του λύκου επανέρχονται — strange, dense, northern. Hard and remarkable.
Τι μένει από τη νύχτα — Cavafy in Paris, as a novel

Contemporary Greek writing.front: The six subjects of contemporary Greek writing
Contemporary Greek writing.back: The crisis; migration and the boats; memory — the civil war, the junta, Asia Minor; Athens as a subject; the island and the village; and family, which is permanent

Kontoglou and the Orthodox writers.back: Romiosyne — the Orthodox Christian Greek people of Byzantium and the Ottoman centuries, defined by the Church rather than by antiquity. As against Ελληνισμός.

Kontoglou and the Orthodox writers.front: What Kontoglou did to Greek religious art
Kontoglou and the Orthodox writers.back: He rejected the western-influenced academic painting that had dominated Greek churches since the eighteenth century and returned to the Byzantine tradition — the whole modern revival of Greek iconography descends from him
Kontoglou's statement of what Romiosyne means — that the Orthodox Greek people, not the Parthenon, is what Greece actually is
Thessaloniki’s writer (1908–1993) — Μητέρα Θεσσαλονίκη, Ο Πεθαμένος και η Ανάσταση. The most Orthodox imagination in modern Greek prose, and difficult.
the six volumes of Λόγοι — transcribed speech, simple vocabulary, short paragraphs. The easiest Orthodox reading in Greek.
Βίος και Λόγοι — on love, on prayer, on children
Saint Sophrony (1896–1993) — a Russian who founded the Monastery of Saint John the Baptist at Tolleshunt Knights, Essex, in 1959; canonised 2019. The main Orthodox monastic centre in Britain.
the catechetical talks from Simonopetra (1934–2019) — more demanding, and very fine

Kontoglou and the Orthodox writers.front: The order to read the Orthodox writers in
Kontoglou and the Orthodox writers.back: Paisios, then Kontoglou’s essays, then Pentzikis — the last after the classical curriculum

Modern Greek theology.front: What happened in twentieth-century Greek theology
Modern Greek theology.back: A generation from the 1930s on set out to replace a theology written on German Protestant and scholastic models with one grounded in the Fathers and the liturgical and ascetic tradition
deification, theosis — and note the ancient -ις ending, used unchanged because the term is the Fathers’ own
hypostasis, person — against η ουσία, essence
the uncreated energies — the Palamite distinction
ancestral sin — NOT "original sin", and the difference is Romanides’ whole argument
sobriety, watchfulness — and ο νηπτικός of the hesychast writers

Modern Greek theology.front: το κατ’ εικόνα και καθ’ ομοίωσιν
Modern Greek theology.back: according to the image and the likeness — Genesis 1:26, and the frame of Orthodox anthropology
hesychasm — and Saint Gregory Palamas, ο Παλαμάς, its defender
Το Προπατορικόν Αμάρτημα, and the Ρωμηοσύνη books — influential and genuinely contested
Metropolitan of Pergamon (1931–2023) — the Church constituted in the Eucharist around the bishop; the most internationally cited Greek theology of the century
Η Ελευθερία του Ήθους, Το Πρόσωπο και ο Έρως (1935–2024) — philosopher as much as theologian, and a newspaper columnist, so his Greek is readable
Panagiotis Nellas — "the deified animal": the human person called to theosis, read out of the Fathers. Short, dense, and where to start.

Modern Greek theology.front: The limit of modern Greek in theology
Modern Greek theology.back: You can read the theology; you cannot yet read the Fathers it quotes — and the discipline consists of reading the Fathers. Every one of these books is a door into the classical curriculum.

The essayists, and the lost centre.back: Zisimos Lorentzatos, 1961 — nominally on Seferis, in fact the argument that modern Greek literature lost its religious centre and replaced it with literature itself

The essayists, and the lost centre.front: Lorentzatos’ candidate for the writer who kept the centre
The essayists, and the lost centre.back: Papadiamantis — the chanter from Skiathos, writing in the Church’s register about the Church’s year, dismissed by the literary establishment of his day
continuity — the great Greek argument: whether modern Greece is continuous with Byzantium, with antiquity, or with neither
westernisation — and whether it was a gain
the critic whose modern Greek Iliad and Odyssey are the standard — and reading Homer in modern Greek translation is a legitimate step
essays on Orthodoxy, modernity and the Greek self — contested and interesting

The essayists, and the lost centre.front: The objections to Lorentzatos worth knowing
The essayists, and the lost centre.back: That Elytis built the Άξιον Εστί on the Liturgy, that Ritsos wrote in the form of the Lamentations, and that Pentzikis and Kontoglou are precisely counter-examples

How Greeks talk about their literature.back: Did you read it in Greek? — the question you will be asked, and answering yes is one of the better moments available to a learner

How Greeks talk about their literature.front: Το έχω αρχίσει και το παράτησα.
How Greeks talk about their literature.back: I started it and gave up.
the language question — demotic against katharevousa, settled in 1976 and still argued about
the single-accent system, which replaced the polytonic in 1982 — still resented by some, and the Church keeps the polytonic in liturgical texts

How Greeks talk about their literature.front: Why literature sits differently in Greek conversation
How Greeks talk about their literature.back: Poetry is quoted, poets are public figures, the national anthem is a poem, the school anthology is shared memory, and the argument about the language is political rather than academic

How Greeks talk about their literature.front: The caution about praising a Greek book
How Greeks talk about their literature.back: Literary opinion is often political opinion — Ritsos and the left, Kazantzakis and the Church, Romanides and national identity. Ask rather than assert.

Ad astra.front: The permanent arrangement, after the curriculum
Ad astra.back: A book always on the go; something in your ears in the dead time; the daily saint; ten minutes of the deck; Greek at church by default; a page a week written; and a poem a month

Ad astra.front: The four things that decay without deliberate maintenance
Ad astra.back: Speaking (the ten minutes a week); writing (a page a week); the accents and spelling (copy a paragraph by hand); and comprehension, which plateaus at the level of what you read
Classical Greek into Koine, Byzantine and liturgical Greek — the hymnography, the Fathers, the Septuagint and the service books. Nothing gates it.

Ad astra.front: The measure of the whole route
Ad astra.back: Not a level. Whether in five years there is Greek in your ordinary week without your having arranged it.

Review: stage 11, and the end of the rou.back: Maps rather than instruction: the poets, the folk tradition, the prose, the Church’s own writers, the arguments — and what to do for the rest of your life

Review: stage 11, and the end of the rou.front: What the whole curriculum has and has not given
Review: stage 11, and the end of the rou.back: Speaking, listening, reading, writing, the dialect and the conversation — and NOT the Liturgy, which it said in its first paragraph and which is the next curriculum

Review: stage 11, and the end of the rou.front: The last instruction of the route
Review: stage 11, and the end of the rou.back: Keep a book going, keep the four-minute floor, speak to someone weekly, and learn a poem a month. Ad astra.

Why the endings carry the leverage.front: Why the endings are where the leverage is
Why the endings carry the leverage.back: Roots are arbitrary and inherited; ENDINGS are decided by the grammar — and endings are where most of the letters are, so getting them right removes most of your errors

Why the endings carry the leverage.front: καλή, καλοί, καλεί — how to tell them apart
Why the endings carry the leverage.back: καλή is a feminine singular adjective; καλοί a masculine plural; καλεί the verb καλώ in the third person. καλί is not a word.

Why the endings carry the leverage.front: The commonest orthographic error in Greek
Why the endings carry the leverage.back: Writing να γράφη for να γράφει. The third person singular of a verb is -ει in every mood; -η is a katharevousa form abolished in 1976.

The masculine endings.back: -ος (omicron), -ης (eta), -ας, -έας, -ους, -ωνας — and -ος with omicron and -ης with eta cover most masculine nouns
Drops the ς and keeps the eta: ο μαθητής → του μαθητή

The masculine endings.front: The plural of every masculine -ος noun
The masculine endings.back: -οι: οι άνθρωποι, οι δρόμοι, οι καλοί — never -ι and never -η
-ους with ς: τους ανθρώπους — the one plural form not shared with the nominative

The feminine endings.front: The single highest-value feminine plural rule
The feminine endings.back: An abstract noun in -ση/-ξη/-ψη makes its plural in -σεις: η απόφαση → οι αποφάσεις, η πόλη → οι πόλεις, η δύναμη → οι δυνάμεις
Adds a ς: της νίκης, της ώρας, της απόφασης
η οδός, η μέθοδος, η είσοδος, η περίοδος, η διάμετρος — feminine articles with masculine-shaped endings, and all learned vocabulary
Identical to the nominative — την νίκη, την ώρα, την πόλη — which removes one decision entirely

The feminine endings.front: The genitive plural of the πόλη type

The neuter endings.back: The nominative and accusative are identical in both numbers, which removes half the decisions
-ιού, with the stress on the ending: το παιδί → του παιδιού, το σπίτι → του σπιτιού
-ατος: το γράμμα → του γράμματος, το μάθημα → του μαθήματος

The neuter endings.front: The plural of a neuter -ος noun
The neuter endings.back: -η with eta: το λάθος → τα λάθη, το κράτος → τα κράτη, το έθνος → τα έθνη. The neuter’s one real trap.
Singular -ι is always iota; singular -ο always omicron; plural -α/-ια/-ατα always alpha; plural -η belongs to the -ος nouns

The genitive, in all three genders.front: The four genitive errors the table prevents
The genitive, in all three genders.back: του μαθητής (drop the ς); της νίκη (add a ς); του παιδίου (it is -ιού); του γράμματου (it is -ατος)

The genitive, in all three genders.front: The genitive plural, in one word
The genitive, in all three genders.back: -ων. Always omega, in all three genders, with no exception worth the name.
του with omicron is the genitive singular; των with omega the genitive plural — two of the commonest words in the language

The genitive, in all three genders.front: The drill that fixes the genitive
The genitive, in all three genders.back: Take any noun phrase and put it after λόγω, μετά or σύμφωνα με, saying the ending’s reason aloud

The plurals, in all three genders.front: The four plural endings that sound alike
The plurals, in all three genders.back: Masculine -ος → -οι; feminine -ση → -εις; neuter -ος → -η; feminine -ος → -οί. All four say *i*.

The plurals, in all three genders.front: The three questions that decide a plural
The plurals, in all three genders.back: What gender? What is the singular ending? Then read the plural off the table.
οι (masc. and fem. nominative, omicron-iota), τα (neuter), των (genitive), τους / τις / τα (accusative)
η γυναίκα → οι γυναίκες (gen. pl. των γυναικών); το κρέας → τα κρέατα; το φως → τα φώτα; το γάλα → τα γάλατα; το γεγονός → τα γεγονότα; ο καφές → οι καφέδες

The adjective endings.front: When the feminine of an -ος adjective is -α
The adjective endings.back: When the stem ends in a vowel: ωραία, νέα, παλιά, κρύα. Everything else takes -η, including the -ρος adjectives: μικρή, καθαρή.
βαθύς, βαρύς, μακρύς, φαρδύς, πλατύς, ελαφρύς, παχύς, δασύς — small, closed, and the -ύ is upsilon
διεθνής, ευγενής, συνεχής, ακριβής, ασφαλής, πλήρης — genitive -ούς, plural -είς, neuter plural -ή

The adjective endings.front: The one rule that catches most adjective errors
The adjective endings.back: An adjective never has a spelling of its own — it has the noun’s. Find the noun, name its gender, number and case.

Spelling drill: the noun in a sentence.back: Fill the blanked ending and say the REASON aloud. The reason transfers; the answer does not.

Spelling drill: the noun in a sentence.front: What your remaining errors should be after Spelling 2 and 3
Spelling drill: the noun in a sentence.back: Roots, accents and double consonants — all memory, all cards. Ending errors should be near zero.

The verb endings, and the -ει problem.back: A verb’s first person is -ω with omega (γράφω); a neuter singular is -ο with omicron (το βιβλίο, καλό)
Identical in sound. Can you put εσείς in front? Then -ετε, active. Can you put αυτό? Then -εται, passive.

The verb endings, and the -ει problem.front: Noun or verb — the one question for every *i*
The verb endings, and the -ει problem.back: η νίκη is a noun, so -η; νικεί is a verb, so -ει. η ζωή / ζει. η τιμή / τιμά.

The present and the -άω verbs.back: -ώ, -άς, -ά, -άμε, -άτε, -ούν — with the alternatives -άω, -άει, -άνε. No -ει anywhere: the third singular is αγαπά or αγαπάει.

The present and the -άω verbs.front: The two questions that identify a conjugation
The present and the -άω verbs.back: Where is the stress in the first person — stem or ending? And is the second person -άς or -είς?
It is the commonest word in the language and it looks like a passive ending without being one
Both types converge in -ούσα: αγαπούσα, μπορούσα — and -ούσα is long enough that no augment is ever needed

The past endings, and the augment.front: The six past endings, shared by the aorist and the imperfect
The past endings, and the augment.back: -α, -ες, -ε, -αμε, -ατε, -αν. Every one has alpha or epsilon and none has an *i* — so the past is the easiest part of the verb to spell.
The past tense’s stress falls on the third syllable from the end. If the word has only two, an ε- is prefixed to make a third: έγραψα but γράψαμε.

The past endings, and the augment.front: The five verbs whose augment is η-
The learned augment, to read not write
The past endings, and the augment.back: Katharevousa puts the ε- inside a compound: ανεχώρησε for αναχώρησε, ενεγράφη for γράφτηκε, εγένετο for έγινε

The perfective stems, spelt.front: The three perfective markers, and what decides them
The perfective stems, spelt.back: Labials (π β φ, and -εύω) give ψ; velars (κ γ χ) give ξ; everything else gives σ
It is a fact about each verb: διαβάζω → διαβάσω but αλλάζω → άλλαξα. Roughly, -ίζω takes σ and -άζω often takes ξ, with exceptions both ways.
-ήσω with eta for the -άω verbs (αγαπήσω, μιλήσω); -έσω with epsilon for some 2b verbs (μπορέσω, καλέσω); -άσω for a small group (γελάσω, περάσω, ξεχάσω, χαλάσω)

The perfective stems, spelt.front: The three irregular aorists with ει in the stem
The perfective stems, spelt.back: έμεινα (μένω), έστειλα (στέλνω) — and έπλυνα (πλένω) with upsilon

The passive endings.back: -μαι, -σαι, -ται, -μαστε, -στε, -νται — and the three vowel-final ones are all -αι, never -ε
-θηκα, -τηκα, -χτηκα, -στηκα, with the person endings -ηκα, -ηκες, -ηκε, -ήκαμε, -ήκατε, -ηκαν. All eta, never iota.
*You consider* (active, second plural) against *it is considered* (passive, third singular). Both common in written Greek.
-θεί with epsilon-iota: να ανακοινωθεί, θα εγκριθεί. NOT -θή, which is katharevousa.
It has no active, so έρχεται, σκέφτεται, φοβάται are the only forms — there is no έρχετε

The subjunctive, which has no spelling o.front: Why the subjunctive has no spelling of its own
