The subjunctive, which has no spelling o.back: Modern Greek has no distinct subjunctive forms — να plus the ordinary indicative endings, in one aspect or the other

The subjunctive, which has no spelling o.front: The katharevousa subjunctive, which is now wrong
The subjunctive, which has no spelling o.back: ίνα γράφη → να γράφει; να γράφωμεν → να γράφουμε; να γραφή → να γραφεί
δεν negates the indicative; μην negates everything with να, and the imperative. There is no negative imperative form.
-τε on the perfective stem: γράψτε, διαβάστε, πάρτε, πείτε, δώστε, ελάτε

Spelling drill: the verb in a sentence.front: The six verb error types to log
Spelling drill: the verb in a sentence.back: -η for -ει; -ετε for -εται; the wrong perfective marker; a missing or wrong augment; -θή for -θεί; the wrong conjugation
Twenty minutes twice a week on a drill set, plus one four-sentence dictation. Forty minutes.

Double consonants.front: Why Greek doubles consonants at all
Double consonants.back: Standard Greek pronounces them as single sounds — the doubling is pure orthography inherited from Ancient Greek. Cypriot still pronounces them long, which is a genuine aid to memory.

Double consonants.front: The one real rule about double consonants
Double consonants.back: A double letter is often a prefix meeting a stem: εκ + κλησία → εκκλησία; συν + γραφέας → συγγραφέας; εν + νοια → έννοια

Double consonants.front: εκκλησία, and why the κκ cannot be forgotten
Double consonants.back: It is εκ + κλησία — *called out* — so the double kappa is a prefix boundary
πολύ (*very, much*) has one lambda; πολλοί, πολλά, πολλές (*many*) have two
μέλι (honey) one lambda; μέλλον (the future) two

The prefixes, and how they assimilate.back: συμ- before π β φ ψ μ; συγ- before κ γ χ ξ; συλ- before λ; συρ- before ρ; συν- otherwise
εμ- before π β φ μ; εγ- before κ γ χ; ελ- before λ; εν- otherwise
εξ- before a vowel (εξέλιξη, εξομολόγηση, εξ αρχής); εκ- before a consonant (έκθεση, εκλογή, εκκλησία)
αν- before a vowel (ανίκανος, ανώμαλος); α- before a consonant (άδικος, άγνωστος)

The prefixes, and how they assimilate.front: The practical payoff of knowing the prefixes
The prefixes, and how they assimilate.back: Split the prefix off an unknown long word and nine times in ten it becomes transparent — αναγνωρίζω = ανα + γνωρίζω; υπογραφή = υπο + γραφή

The prefixes, and how they assimilate.front: Why ευ- is spelt ευ even when it sounds like *ef*
The prefixes, and how they assimilate.back: It is the digraph, voiced before a voiced sound (ευλογία) and voiceless before a voiceless one (ευχαριστώ) — spelt ευ either way

The root spellings, by pattern.front: The one real rule about αι inside a root
The root spellings, by pattern.back: Verbs in -αίνω all take αι: μαθαίνω, πεθαίνω, ανεβαίνω, κατεβαίνω, πηγαίνω, ζεσταίνω, παθαίνω, φαίνομαι

The root spellings, by pattern.front: Why the υ words are worth learning as a group
The root spellings, by pattern.back: υ is the least-guessed of the *i* spellings, and the group is large: τύχη, ύλη, φύση, λύση, μύθος, ρυθμός, σύστημα, ξύλο, νύχτα, δύναμη, ψυχή

The root spellings, by pattern.front: The free mnemonic that comes with every lookup
The root spellings, by pattern.back: The etymology line in the Triantafyllidis dictionary. τύχη < τυγχάνω explains the upsilon.

The root spellings, by pattern.front: The four-step method for a root spelling
The root spellings, by pattern.back: Apply the endings rules; split off the prefix; guess the root and check it in Triantafyllidis; card it if you were wrong

Homophones, and spelling as meaning.back: ο τοίχος is the wall of a room or house; το τείχος is a fortification — the walls of Constantinople are τα Τείχη
κλίνω is to incline, and to decline a noun; κλείνω is to close
φιλί is a kiss; φυλή a tribe or race
As simply as the sound allows, since 1976: single consonants, ε rather than αι, ι rather than ει or υ — τρένο, σεζόν, μπάσκετ, σάντουιτς
ότι means *that*; ό,τι with the comma means *whatever*. The comma is required.

Spelling drill: dictation.front: Why dictation is the best single spelling exercise
Spelling drill: dictation.back: It tests the endings, the roots, the accents, final -ν and the double consonants all at once — and the listening with them
Two to four sentences of audio you can follow; play it twice writing by hand; a third time to check; then classify every error
The Ellinomatheia listening papers — graded A1 to C2, with audio and transcripts
Not perfection, which no Greek has: no ending errors, accents placed, and a known list of root words on cards

Abbreviations, in full.back: Ιερός Ναός — Holy Church of…, and it begins every Greek church notice
πατήρ — Fr, before a priest’s name
Ιερά Μονή (Holy Monastery) or Ιερά Μητρόπολις (Holy Metropolis)
προ / μετά Χριστού — BC / AD, with a capital Χ for Christ
Παλαιά / Καινή Διαθήκη — Old / New Testament
Ματθ. 5, 3–12 or Ματθ. 5:3–12 — the comma is the more traditional Greek form
They are written in capitals, and a word in capitals takes no accents

The numerals, in full.front: The only four numerals that decline
The numerals, in full.back: ένας, τρεις, τέσσερις, and the hundreds and thousands. Everything from 5 to 199 is invariable.
τριών and τεσσάρων — τριών ημερών, τεσσάρων ετών
Units, tens and hundreds each have a letter and are added: ιβ΄ = 12, κε΄ = 25, ρν΄ = 150. A keraia (΄) marks a numeral.

The numerals, in full.front: The three letters that survive only as numerals
The numerals, in full.back: ϛ stigma (6, also στ΄), ϙ koppa (90), ϡ sampi (900) — not letters of the alphabet

The numerals, in full.front: Where you will meet alphabetic numerals
The numerals, in full.back: The odes of a canon (ωδή α΄, γ΄), the tones (ήχος πλ. δ΄), the Councils (η Ζ΄ Οικουμενική), school years, kings and patriarchs
The month in the genitive: 14 Οκτωβρίου 2026 — and 1η for the first

Capitalisation, hyphens and syllables.front: The capitalisation difference learners get wrong most
Capitalisation, hyphens and syllables.back: Language names and nationality adjectives are LOWER CASE in Greek: μαθαίνω ελληνικά, ένα ελληνικό βιβλίο — but ο Έλληνας is capitalised

Capitalisation, hyphens and syllables.front: What a Greek book title capitalises
Capitalisation, hyphens and syllables.back: Only the first word: Το τρίτο στεφάνι
Capitalised: ο Θεός, ο Κύριος, η Παναγία, η Εκκλησία (institution), η Θεία Λειτουργία, the feasts, ο Άγιος Νικόλαος. Lower case: η εκκλησία (building), ο ιερέας, η νηστεία.
Two consonants between vowels go with the following vowel if a Greek word can begin with that pair (βι-βλί-ο); otherwise they split (άν-θρω-πος)
Only when there is no accent to separate the vowels: Μάιος and καΐκι need one, ρολόι does not

Typing and writing Greek, as reference.front: The five non-phonetic keys on the Greek layout
Typing and writing Greek, as reference.back: c = ψ, j = ξ, u = θ, v = ω, w = ς — and q = ; the question mark
Press ; (the semicolon key) then the vowel. shift + ; then the vowel gives the diaeresis.

Typing and writing Greek, as reference.front: The Hyprland setting for a Greek layout
Typing and writing Greek, as reference.back: kb_layout = us,gr with kb_options = grp:alt_shift_toggle — alt + shift switches

Typing and writing Greek, as reference.front: The letters that descend below the line
Typing and writing Greek, as reference.back: γ, η, μ, ρ, φ, χ, ψ, ζ, β, ξ — and the next letter starts from the baseline, not from the tail
Liturgical texts, and the classical curriculum. Not this one.

The spelling checklist, and self-testing.back: Read aloud; count the accents; every *i* — is it an ending?; every *o* — verb or noun?; every *e* — active or passive?; final -ν; the agreement chain; the genitive endings; the perfective marker; the double consonants; the punctuation; read aloud again

The spelling checklist, and self-testing.front: The target distribution of errors after a year of the track
The spelling checklist, and self-testing.back: Endings near zero; accents occasional; roots the bulk, all on cards; double consonants a known list; final -ν near zero

The spelling checklist, and self-testing.front: What the Spelling track cannot do
The spelling checklist, and self-testing.back: Make the roots derivable, because they are not. ποτέ, τύχη, θάλασσα, εκκλησία are facts — meet them, get them wrong, card them.

How the Greek verb is organised.front: The axis the Greek verb is organised on
How the Greek verb is organised.back: Aspect FIRST, tense second. Two stems — imperfective and perfective — and the tense and mood are built on whichever you chose.

How the Greek verb is organised.front: The one empty cell in the Greek verb
How the Greek verb is organised.back: There is no perfective present — you cannot describe something as a completed whole while it is happening

How the Greek verb is organised.front: The five things Greek does not have
How the Greek verb is organised.back: No infinitive; no perfective present; no separate subjunctive forms; no progressive auxiliary; no sequence of tenses in reported speech

How the Greek verb is organised.front: The two questions to ask of any Greek verb form
How the Greek verb is organised.back: Which stem? Which tense and mood? That is how the system is indexed.
έχω or είχα plus an INVARIABLE perfective form that never changes for person: έχω γράψει, έχεις γράψει, έχει γράψει

The two conjugations, in full.back: It has passive-shaped endings and no active, and είναι is the third person for BOTH singular and plural — unique in the language

The two conjugations, in full.front: The verbs that take both conjugation-2 sets
The two conjugations, in full.back: ζητώ, κρατώ, βοηθώ, τραβώ — and both are correct

The two conjugations, in full.front: How to drill a conjugation table
The two conjugations, in full.back: Cover the forms, say all six aloud, uncover and check, redo the misses three times. Thirty seconds a verb.

The imperfect, in full.front: The six uses of the imperfect
The imperfect, in full.back: Background; habit; an ongoing action interrupted; description in the past; an attempt; and politeness (ήθελα να σας ρωτήσω)
Έγραφα ένα γράμμα — I was writing one, perhaps unfinished. Έγραψα ένα γράμμα — I wrote it, done.

The imperfect, in full.front: The two irregular imperfects to know cold
The imperfect, in full.back: ήμουν, ήσουν, ήταν… (είμαι) and είχα, είχες, είχε… (έχω) — and είχα is also the pluperfect’s auxiliary

The imperfective future, subjunctive and.back: θα plus the present, unchanged. θα is invariable and unaccented.

The imperfective future, subjunctive and.front: The verbs with no perfective future
The imperfective future, subjunctive and.back: είμαι, έχω, ξέρω, θέλω, αγαπώ — states rather than events, so their future is naturally imperfective
θα plus the imperfect: θα έγραφα, *I would write* — the politeness tense

The imperfective future, subjunctive and.front: The whole imperfective system, in one line
The imperfective future, subjunctive and.back: One stem, six constructions, and only two sets of endings — the present’s and the past’s

είμαι, έχω, and the state verbs.back: It is a state, and states have no perfective aspect. Where English says *I was*, Greek says ήμουν — the imperfect — and there is nothing else to choose.
μπορώ is *I am able*; μπόρεσα is *I managed*. The aspect difference is a capacity against an occasion.

είμαι, έχω, and the state verbs.front: έπρεπε, and the English modal it covers
είμαι, έχω, and the state verbs.back: Both *I had to go* and *I should have gone* — context decides. And πρέπει να πήγε is *he must have gone*, for inference.

είμαι, έχω, and the state verbs.front: The verbs whose two aspects are two different English verbs
είμαι, έχω, and the state verbs.back: μαθαίνω/μάθω (learn / find out); βλέπω/δω (watch / catch sight of); θυμάμαι/θυμηθώ (hold in mind / recall); καταλαβαίνω/καταλάβω (understand / realise)

How to use a conjugation table.front: The four questions for recognising a verb form
How to use a conjugation table.back: Active or passive? Which tense? Which person? What is the verb? — and Lexiscope when that fails
One sentence into past, imperfect, future, plural, negative, subjunctive, perfect, passive and pluperfect passive — every cell of the table, in two minutes

How to use a conjugation table.front: The eight verb forms to drill, in priority order
How to use a conjugation table.back: Present; aorist and imperfect; θα and να with both stems; είμαι/έχω/πάω/λέω/τρώω; aorist passive; perfect; imperatives; participles

The perfective stem, formed.front: How a perfective is cited in a dictionary
The perfective stem, formed.back: As the first person perfective subjunctive without να — γράψω

The perfective stem, formed.front: Why the three markers are what they are
The perfective stem, formed.back: The same assimilation as English *scribe / script*: a consonant meeting a sibilant. Labials give ψ, velars ξ, everything else σ.
Many form it by dropping the -ν- or changing the stem vowel rather than adding a marker: μένω/μείνω, στέλνω/στείλω, πλένω/πλύνω, φέρνω/φέρω, παίρνω/πάρω
Every verb is carded as a PAIR — γράφω / γράψω on one card. A verb without its perfective is half a verb.

The irregular perfectives.back: δω, πω, βρω, μπω, βγω, πιω — the strangest forms in the language and the most used
Drop the -αιν- and the perfective is short: μαθαίνω/μάθω, παθαίνω/πάθω, καταλαβαίνω/καταλάβω, μπαίνω/μπω, βγαίνω/βγω
A compound inherits its simple verb’s perfective — so thirty simple verbs give you several hundred compounds
προσέλθω, επανέλθω, διέλθω, εξέλθω, εισέλθω — all from έρχομαι, all formal, all in official and church Greek

The aorist, in full.front: Why the aorist and imperfect share their endings
The aorist, in full.back: They do: -α, -ες, -ε, -αμε, -ατε, -αν. The difference between έγραφα and έγραψα is the STEM alone.

The aorist, in full.front: Why the augment is not a separate thing to remember
The aorist, in full.back: It is a consequence of the stress rule: the stress falls on the third syllable from the end, so short stems get an ε- to supply one

The aorist, in full.front: The irregular aorists whose stress does not move
The aorist, in full.back: είδα, είπα, πήγα, πήρα, βρήκα, ήρθα, μπήκα, βγήκα — the commonest verbs, and invariant in stress

The aorist, in full.front: The two aorist errors learners make
The aorist, in full.back: Using the aorist for description (Ήταν ψηλός, not an aorist); and the imperfect for a completed event (Πήγα, not πήγαινα)

The perfective future, subjunctive and i.front: The particles that decide the aspect for you — perfective
The perfective future, subjunctive and i.back: πριν, μόλις, αφού (after), ώσπου, όταν (once, in the future)

The perfective future, subjunctive and i.front: The particles that decide the aspect for you — imperfective
The perfective future, subjunctive and i.back: ενώ, όσο, καθώς, όταν (whenever), πάντα, συνήθως, κάθε, συχνά
The first is *stop writing*; the second *don’t write this*. There is no negative imperative form — μην plus the ordinary verb.
The plural, used to one person: Περιμένετε, παρακαλώ. Καθίστε.

The aspect pairs: the hundred verbs.front: How to use the hundred-verb list
The aspect pairs: the hundred verbs.back: Not by reading. Card them ten at a time as pairs, and check with the cover-and-say drill.
προσεύχομαι/προσευχηθώ, νηστεύω/νηστέψω, εξομολογούμαι/εξομολογηθώ, κοινωνώ/κοινωνήσω, ευλογώ/ευλογήσω, ψάλλω/ψάλω, προσκυνώ/προσκυνήσω, μετανοώ/μετανοήσω

Drilling the pairs.front: Why the pair drill is the highest-value two minutes in the track
Drilling the pairs.back: The aspect choice is made BEFORE the tense, in the instant of speaking — so fluency in Greek is largely fluency in the two stems
For each verb say the present, the aorist, the perfective future and the perfective subjunctive. Ten verbs, forty forms, three minutes.
Two minutes of the pair drill and two of a transformation drill daily, plus two twenty-minute table sessions a week

Drilling the pairs.front: The marker that the Forms track is finished
Drilling the pairs.back: You produce any form without pausing, you recognise the irregulars on sight, and the aspect choice is automatic

The passive present and imperfect.front: The three senses of the Greek passive
The passive present and imperfect.back: True passive (το γράμμα γράφτηκε); reflexive (πλένομαι, ντύνομαι, σηκώνομαι); and reciprocal (αγαπιόμαστε, μιλιόμαστε)

The passive present and imperfect.front: Which passive sense is commonest in speech
The passive present and imperfect.back: The reflexive — which is why so many verbs of daily routine are passive in form: σηκώνομαι, πλένομαι, ντύνομαι, ετοιμάζομαι, κουράζομαι, κοιμάμαι

The passive present and imperfect.front: How Greek names the agent of a passive
The passive present and imperfect.back: από plus the accusative — γράφτηκε από τον Παπαδιαμάντη. And υπό plus the genitive in the learned register, which you read and do not write.

The passive present and imperfect.front: The genuine ambiguity in the passive
The passive present and imperfect.back: The first person plural is identical in the present and the imperfect: γραφόμαστε

The aorist passive.back: -ήθηκα/-ώθηκα for conjugation 2 and the -ώνω verbs; -φτηκα for labial stems; -χτηκα for velar; -θηκα/-στηκα for the rest
Register. The plainer forms are modern and safer; the -φθ-/-χθ- forms are commoner in official and church writing.
The modern aorist passive against the ancient one, kept because it is the Church’s word for a saint’s death
-ώ, -είς, -εί, -ούμε, -είτε, -ούν on the -θ- stem: να ανακοινωθεί, θα εγκριθεί

The perfect tenses.front: Why the compound tenses are the easiest forms in the verb
The perfect tenses.back: Only έχω conjugates. The second word — γράψει — never changes for person, number or gender.

The perfect tenses.front: How much Greek uses the perfect
The perfect tenses.back: Far less than English. Έφαγα ήδη, not έχω φάει; Είδες την ταινία;, not έχεις δει.

The perfect tenses.front: The four jobs the Greek perfect does keep
The perfect tenses.back: Lifetime experience; something never done (δεν έχω πάει ποτέ); emphasising completion against expectation; and precision about sequence in writing

The perfect tenses.front: The English present perfect that is PRESENT in Greek
The perfect tenses.back: With *for* or *since*: Μένω εδώ δέκα χρόνια. Μαθαίνω ελληνικά εδώ και δύο χρόνια. If it is still happening, use the present.
έχω plus a DECLINED -μένος participle, agreeing with the object: *I have the letter written, ready*. Common in speech and in no textbook.

The participles.front: Why there is no perfective active participle
The participles.back: There is not — γράψοντας does not exist. Greek uses έχοντας plus the invariable perfective: έχοντας διαβάσει.
-οντας with omicron for conjugation 1; -ώντας with omega for conjugation 2, because the stress is on it

The participles.front: Why γραμμένος has a double μ
The participles.back: The labial stem assimilates: γράφω → γραμμένος, κρύβω → κρυμμένος, κόβω → κομμένος

The participles.front: The three ways to form a passive participle
The participles.back: Labial stem → -μμένος (γραμμένος, κομμένος); velar → -γμένος (ανοιγμένος, βρεγμένος); dental or σ → -σμένος (διαβασμένος, κλεισμένος); conjugation 2 → -ημένος / -ωμένος

The participles.front: The learned participles you CAN use
The participles.back: The naturalised -όμενος nouns: ο εργαζόμενος, ο ενδιαφερόμενος, ο προϊστάμενος, τα λεγόμενα, τα δεδομένα, το περιεχόμενο

The full verb, on one page.front: How many forms the Greek verb has
The full verb, on one page.back: About seventy, from four stems, with two sets of endings for the active and two for the passive — smaller than the Romance systems

The full verb, on one page.front: Which verb forms are ninety per cent of use
The full verb, on one page.back: Present active, aorist active, imperfect active, θα and να with both active stems, γράφεται and γράφτηκε

The full verb, on one page.front: The one-page exercise worth doing once
The full verb, on one page.back: Copy the full table of one regular verb out by hand — twenty minutes, and it drills the handwriting and the spelling at once

The full verb, on one page.front: How much of the table an irregular verb actually changes
The full verb, on one page.back: βλέπω / δω differs from γράφω / γράψω in four cells out of seventy

Deponents, and the verbs with no active.front: What a deponent is, and the test
Deponents, and the verbs with no active.back: A verb that exists only in passive endings with an active meaning. If the active does not exist — there is no έρχω — the verb is deponent.
φοβάμαι, θυμάμαι, κοιμάμαι, λυπάμαι — four verbs, one pattern, all very common: -άμαι, -άσαι, -άται, -όμαστε, -άστε, -ούνται
προσεύχομαι, εξομολογούμαι, εύχομαι, δέχομαι — and μετανοώ, which is active in form and belongs with them in sense
σηκώνω/σηκώνομαι, ντύνω/ντύνομαι, πλένω/πλένομαι, ετοιμάζω/ετοιμάζομαι, κουράζω/κουράζομαι, χάνω/χάνομαι, βρίσκω/βρίσκομαι, φέρνω/φέρομαι

The numerals and the pronouns, as refere.front: The order of the weak pronouns
The numerals and the pronouns, as refere.back: Indirect before direct, and both before the verb: μου το έδωσε. After the verb in the imperative: δώσε μου το. Cypriot puts them after the verb everywhere.
With a noun: ο εαυτός μου, which declines — Αγαπώ τον εαυτό μου. Greek has no reflexive pronoun.

The numerals and the pronouns, as refere.front: Why Greek has no possessive adjective
The numerals and the pronouns, as refere.back: The genitive clitic does the work, placed AFTER the noun: το σπίτι μου, ο πατέρας της, τα παιδιά τους

The irregular nouns and adjectives.front: The five nouns with an -ατος or -ότος genitive
The irregular nouns and adjectives.back: το φως/του φωτός, το γάλα/του γάλακτος, το κρέας/του κρέατος, το γεγονός/του γεγονότος, το καθεστώς/του καθεστώτος

The irregular nouns and adjectives.front: The Greek nouns with no singular
The irregular nouns and adjectives.back: τα Χριστούγεννα, τα Θεοφάνεια, τα γενέθλια, τα μεσάνυχτα, τα λεφτά, οι διακοπές — hence Καλά Χριστούγεννα, with a plural adjective

The irregular nouns and adjectives.front: The -εως genitive, and where you will meet it
The irregular nouns and adjectives.back: The learned form of the -ση nouns: ημερομηνία γεννήσεως, η Κυριακή της Αναστάσεως, ώρα ενάρξεως. The commonest learned form on any form, sign or church notice. Read it; write the -ης.
The modern and the learned forms of the same word — which is why the Elders’ books say Γέροντας Παΐσιος and a liturgical text has του γέροντος

The irregular nouns and adjectives.front: The one genuinely irregular Greek adjective
The irregular nouns and adjectives.back: πολύς, πολλή, πολύ — single λ in the masculine and neuter nominative singular, double λ everywhere else
καλός→καλύτερος, κακός→χειρότερος, πολύς→περισσότερος, λίγος→λιγότερος, μεγάλος→μεγαλύτερος, μικρός→μικρότερος

The irregular verbs, in one list.back: Nine verbs on one pattern: σέρνω/σύρω, γέρνω/γείρω, δέρνω/δείρω, σπέρνω/σπείρω, φέρνω/φέρω, παίρνω/πάρω, στέλνω/στείλω, πλένω/πλύνω, μένω/μείνω

The irregular verbs, in one list.front: The eleven learned aorists to recognise on sight
The irregular verbs, in one list.back: εγένετο, ήλθε, είπεν/έφη, έδωκε, εγράφη, εκοιμήθη, ανέστη, ετελέσθη, εβαπτίσθη, απεβίωσε, επορεύθη
*It is going to, it is a matter of* — third person singular only, and very common in formal Greek: Πρόκειται να γίνει αύριο.

The irregular verbs, in one list.front: The whole irregularity of the Greek verb, counted
The irregular verbs, in one list.back: Thirty core irregulars, nine on the -ερνω pattern, a dozen impersonals, and eleven learned forms to recognise — against English’s two hundred strong verbs

When a form defeats you.front: The five steps for an unknown Greek form
When a form defeats you.back: Find the ending; ask what kind of ending it is; strip it and look at the stem; strip the prefix; and put it through Lexiscope

When a form defeats you.front: What the Forms track cannot cover
When a form defeats you.back: The learned forms, which are everywhere in church, legal and official texts. For those: identify the root, accept the approximate sense, move on — and that is where the next curriculum begins.

When a form defeats you.front: The one habit that makes the Forms track stick
When a form defeats you.back: Two minutes of the pair drill and one transformation drill a day. The tables are reference; the drills are the learning.
